fatal_errors: The proposed intervention—adding an unspecified HEA reinforcement—is not the target intervention of liquid-metal dealloying a directionally segregated WTaVTi precursor in molten Cu.
The initial material is incorrectly treated as an existing W–Cu composite rather than an as-cast WTaVTi alloy with sacrificial Ti/V-rich interdendritic channels.
The hypothesis omits the essential 1200 °C, 96 h processing condition and the selective replacement that forms bicontinuous RHEA ligaments and Cu channels.
The proposed mechanism does not describe preferential Ti extraction, Cu ingress, retention of W/Ta/V, or formation of the approximately 300 nm W-rich passivating interlayer.
The cited evidence concerns HEA-reinforced Al or Mg composites and TiC-reinforced W; it does not support improved thermal conductivity or suppression of voids in this WTaVTi–Cu system.
The irradiation claim is not bounded to 25 keV He+ testing of precursor dendrites as a proxy and incorrectly implies validation under general irradiation conditions.
explanation: The response recognizes the broad W/Cu joining problem and predicts higher thermal conductivity, but it does not reconstruct the material, intervention, mechanism, conditions, or measured comparisons. The hidden work creates a directionally aligned RHEA–Cu composite by molten-Cu dealloying of a segregated WTaVTi precursor, rather than by adding an HEA reinforcement to W–Cu. Its thermal baseline is chiefly the low-conductivity precursor, with pure W, pure Cu, and conventional W–Cu as additional controls; irradiation performance is compared with pure W and related alloys. The proposed experiment could test a generic reinforcement effect, but lacks specified composition, processing, temperature range, irradiation protocol, interfacial characterization, and controls needed to distinguish the target mechanism. The supporting citations are materially and functionally remote and do not establish the claimed thermal benefit.
